newsitem.title: USA: U.S. court hears arguments on key tobacco suit.
newsitem.headline: U.S. court hears arguments on key tobacco suit.

text.p: A federal court judge Thursday heard arguments on whether a major lawsuit against tobacco companies on behalf of nearly three million Pennsylvania smokers should be allowed to proceed as a class action.
An attorney for the smokers contended that the suit should move forward, which would make it the first such suit against the tobacco industry to win federal court certification as a class action.

A lawyer representing the tobacco industry, however, argued that recent federal court decisions made clear the class action should be thrown out -- that the numerous individual issues involved made it impossible to consider the group as a class.

"It's awfully plain what our federal judiciary is telling us -- mass tort (civil) cases shouldn't be certified. There are too many individual issues," said Robert Heim, an attorney for Philip Morris Co Inc.

Heim argued on behalf of all of the tobacco companies named in the suit filed in August 1996. The suit alleges the companies lied about the addictive nature of cigarettes and deliberately sought to hook young people on smoking.
The suit asks that the companies pay for continued medical monitoring of the state's smokers and seeks repayment of the money spent by smokers for cigarettes.
Such medical monitoring could cost $1,000 to $3,000 on average for each of the 2.5 to 2.8 million Pennsylvania smokers covered in the suit, plaintiffs attorney Dianne Nast told the court.
Reimbursable costs for cigarettes could reach as high as $350,000 for a 50-year smoker, when interest on the money spent on smoking is added in, Nast said.

In the wake of a federal appeals court decision last year rejecting a national class action suit filed in Louisiana, several cases have been filed similar to the Pennsylvania one on a state-by-state basis.
Nast said there were now about 20 such state cases, plus 20-25 suits by state attorneys general seeking to recover smoking-related costs to public treasuries.
Two class action suits have been certified in Florida state courts, and a state court in Louisiana is currently considering certification, smokers' attorney Stephen Sheller said.
U.S. District Court Judge Clarence Newcomer, who is in charge of the Pennsylvania case, gave no indication of when he would rule, but Sheller said he expected the judge would act quickly.
During the three-hour long court session Thursday, Newcomer asked several skeptical questions regarding the tobacco company's arguments.

Told by Heim that, if the case proceeded as a class action, the plaintiffs would have an unmanageable burden of proving each smoker in the class smoked for reasons other than personal choice, Newcomer said the plaintiffs would be entitled to use expert testimony to try to make that case.

Heim repeatedly cited the recent appeals court decisions on class actions -- both the rejection of the national class action smoking case and the rejection of a settlement in a massive class action asbestos case -- as indications large, complex class action suits were no longer acceptable.
He said the smokers should, if they felt they had cause for suits, be required to bring them individually against the tobacco companies.

But Nast said the appeals court decisions involved different issues, and the Pennsylvania smokers' case pertained to more focused issues which could readily be resolved treating the group as one class. "It's not so large as to be unmanageable," she said.
Sheller said no decision had been made on whether the suit would proceed on behalf of seven named plaintiffs if the class action certification were rejected.
